To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the emergence of drug tolerance and genetic resistance in M. tuberculosis is mediated by stress responses that protect the bacillus from environmental and immune-mediated DNA damage.

(i) the bacillary DNA damage and stress response pathways might contribute to the generation of antibiotic resistance mutations; (ii) the stringent response alarmones, (p) ppGpp, might contribute to the emergence of persisters; and (iii) the stringent response might be targeted by the anti-TB drug isoniazid.

(1) the DNA repair system is a major determinant of the efficacy of frontline anti-Tuberculosis drugs, (2) the stringent response is a major determinant in the emergence of persisters, and (3) the stringent response might also be a major determinant of antibiotic resistance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the molecular mechanisms that enable M. tuberculosis to survive the stress of infection and, in so doing, to subvert chemotherapy.
understanding how M. tuberculosis responds to stress, and how this influences drug efficacy.

the elucidation of the genetic and biochemical mechanisms that enable bacillary adaptation to hostile in vivo environments, and the identification of novel targets and approaches for the treatment of active TB infection and the prevention of disease relapse.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the failure of current anti-TB drug combinations to cure TB disease is multifactorial, and that the development of new therapeutic strategies must take into account the complex interactions between bacillary and host factors that influence drug efficacy.
the TB chemotherapy problem is not a single problem, but a collection of different problems, each of which requires its own solution.

the failure of anti-TB drug regimens is not solely a consequence of the emergence of drug resistance but is also due to the operation of a variety of mechanisms that subvert drug action, including the generation of antibiotic-resistant variants, the emergence of persisters, and the development of tolerance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the current frontline TB drug combination has been shown to be suboptimal in terms of sterilizing the bacilli, and that there is a strong likelihood of the emergence of persisters as a result of the operation of the stringent response.

we have shown that the stringent response is important for the survival of Mycobacterium smegmatis and Mycobacterium bovis BCG under conditions of nutrient deprivation, and that the stringent response contributes to the survival of M. tuberculosis under the same conditions.
the bacilli are exposed not just to antibiotics but also to other stresses, such as DNA damage, and the bacilli are able to respond to these stresses by activating different pathways.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the current anti-TB chemotherapy paradigm is unlikely to be effective against the majority of M. tuberculosis infections.

the failure of frontline TB drugs might reflect a combination of genetic and non-genetic tolerance mechanisms that are likely to operate in parallel and in concert with each other, thereby rendering the current chemotherapy strategy ineffective.

the failure of frontline drugs to sterilize M. tuberculosis infections is not due to genetic resistance but rather to the ability of bacilli to survive the drug stress through the operation of stress response pathways.
